WASHINGTON — A divided Supreme Court has cleared the way for President Trump to finish building his new White House ballroom with mostly private money and without approval from Congress.
By a 5-4 vote, the justices granted an emergency appeal from Trump and his lawyers on Monday, setting aside a judge’s order that would stop the construction.
But Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. dissented, along with the court’s three liberals.
Roberts said the construction project was “likely unlawful” and should not be allowed to continue.
“The White House is not just any building ... when it comes to historic preservation,” Roberts wrote. “Winston Churchill once remarked that ‘[w]e shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us.’ All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People’s House.”
The outcome turned on the standing of the plaintiffs, the National Trust for Historic Preservation and its members.
The conservative majority pointed to Alison Hoagland, one of its members, who said she lives in Washington, walks by the White House about once a month and said she found the “scale,” “height” and “massing” of the huge ballroom to be distasteful.
“This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury,” the unsigned order said.
Trump has responded to growing legal and political obstacles to his ballroom, arch and other projects by attempting to force approvals through faster than opponents can challenge them.
It is a major victory for Trump, whose ballroom project has become a signature effort of his second term and a political lightning rod in Washington, where Republicans have refused to fund it with public money.
Trump celebrated the victory with a post on social media, declaring the venue would now be built “without any further contingency, doubt, or threat.”
“We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of.”
The massive new structure, set to dwarf the historic White House mansion, is the president’s singular vision — one of a string of aesthetic projects Trump has pursued in a feverish effort to cement his legacy by putting his personal stamp on the nation’s capital.
But preservationists and architects have criticized the proposed ballroom as a garish, rushed project that ignored the input of experts. The president has personally overruled his own chosen architects after being told the building would overwhelm the executive complex.
Democrats have seized on the president’s fixation on the ballroom as a symbol of vanity and detachment from the concerns of everyday Americans heading into November’s midterm elections.
According to recent polls, a bipartisan majority of voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the economy and say the country is facing an affordability crisis. The ballroom is projected to cost more than $400 million, excluding the undisclosed cost of underground security upgrades.
Trump’s three appointees — Justices Neil M. Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — joined conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito in an unsigned opinion ruling for the president.
The conservative majority also said Trump and his appointees had stressed the new ballroom was needed for national security and said the lower courts judges should not have interfered.
California officials stressed that the court’s ruling does not allow final implementation of the new rules requested by Trump.
Administration officials have argued that an underground “integrated military complex” was the heart of the project and that the ballroom would merely be sit top of the facility “vitally required by national security.”
The decision is not a final ruling, but it gives a green light to Trump’s go-it-alone approach, which is in keeping with his history as a hotel builder.
He believed the White House needed a grand ballroom that could seat hundreds of dignitaries. Acting on his own, he ordered the East Wing torn down in October to make room of his larger ballroom.
He also said most of the project would be paid for by private donations.
But the Constitution gave Congress the power to manage property belonging to the United States. A 1912 law says new buildings “shall not erected ... on public grounds within the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”
Trump chose to ignore the law and did not seek approval from Congress, which is led by Republicans.
The Republican president’s lawyers had asked the justices to reconsider their refusal to hear his appeal. The court denied Trump’s petition along with several others.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued in December, contending Trump was a “temporary tenant, not the owner” of the White House.
U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ruled Trump had no authority to build a ballroom on the White House grounds without the approval of Congress, and he ordered a halt to the above-ground construction.
The District of Columbia Circuit Court affirmed his decision by a 2-1 vote.
“Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People’s House — to fit a particular President’s desires,” wrote Judge Patricia Millett for the appeals court.
Trump’s lawyers sent a fast-track appeal to the Supreme Court on Aug. 14.
The court’s majority allowed Trump to fend off the legal challenge by concluding the historic preservationists could not show they were harmed by  the huge new ballroom.

OpenAI has been at the centre of new concerns over uncontrolled AI activity
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.
AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.
The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme.
Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.
OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".
But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.
When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.
OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.
However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.
In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.
Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.
The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.
Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."
It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.
Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.
In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.
In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.
OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.
"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.
Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.
"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."
Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?
Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it?
The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet.
OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after an incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being prompted to do so.
Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later.
Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, during a United Nations Security Council session on AI on Wednesday: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly."
"Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added.
During that same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the head of rival firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to form global standards for AI safety and ways to monitor and report such incidents.
Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack
While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as the BBC has reported .
OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred.
"Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete."
David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents.
He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development.
"We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said.

articles.title_zh: The other crop that built China: how millet became foundation for Chinese civilisation
articles.content_orig:
While domestication of rice was crucial in southern China, it was millet that ruled the North, laying groundwork for birth of the country
Rice may be the most universal ingredient in the world, serving as a cornerstone of the diet for billions in Asia.
However, for much of Chinese history, rice faced a serious competitor, and entire cultures developed around a different cereal grain, one that has since diminished in significance: millet.
Millet is a cereal grain that behaves and tastes similarly to rice but has a rounder form. It is often used in porridge, stir-fries, or even fritters. In certain regions of China, millet is favoured as a food for pregnant women, with millet porridge being particularly gentle on the stomach. Despite this, it cannot rival the cultural importance of rice.
Yet, the domestication of millet, along with other cereals globally, stands as one of the most pivotal events in human history. Its domestication fundamentally altered natural landscapes and enabled humans to control the plants they consume, as opposed to surviving at the mercy of wild crops.

articles.title_orig: Remote section of China’s Great Wall damaged by 20 years of mine waste dumping
articles.title_zh: Remote section of China’s Great Wall damaged by 20 years of mine waste dumping
articles.content_orig:
Whistle-blowers were repeatedly ignored as mining interests removed Ming dynasty stones to create a short cut to slag dump, CCTV reports
While foreign leaders and their families walk the iconic restored sections of the Great Wall around Beijing, the ancient stones of a remote Ming-era stretch of the structure in northern central China have been sacrificed for cheaper dumping of coal-mining waste.
For nearly 20 years, a section of the wall in Ningwu county, Shanxi province, was used as a short cut to dump slag, despite whistle-blowers repeatedly raising the alarm to officials, according to a report by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The damage to the Great Wall’s Guojiayao section began in 2007, when an unlicensed miner, Ningwu Chaokai Coal Industry, dug a trench through the structure as a way to dispose of excavation waste, the report said.
In 2013, Shenda Chaokai Coal Industry was established through the consolidation of multiple mining teams and continued using the breach to dump slag, bypassing the long mountain roads.

articles.title_orig: Tensions run high in Northern Ireland after contentious march given go-ahead
articles.title_zh: Tensions run high in Northern Ireland after contentious march given go-ahead
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of protesters have blocked a route into the Catholic area of a Northern Irish town that a Protestant organisation was due to march down.
Northern Ireland’s High Court permitted the Protestant Orange Order organisation to march through a mainly Catholic area in the town of Portadown on Sunday for the first time in 28 years, reviving one of the region’s most contentious marching disputes.
The court rejected a final attempt by residents to stop the parade from passing through the Garvaghy Road, after Northern Ireland’s Court of Appeal overturned a temporary injunction granted on Saturday.
Thousands of people, including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill of the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein and the party’s ‌leader, Mary Lou McDonald, gathered on the road to protest against the decision.
“This is madness,” McDonald told reporters shortly after 8am (07:00 GMT) when the march was due to begin. “This, in fact, is primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.
“This is a ⁠dignified and united community, and they are absolutely determined that ⁠they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”
McDonald and O’Neill urged the British government and police to intervene to stop the parade. O’Neill said she ⁠had spoken to Britain’s minister for the region and the Irish government.
Police vans parked nearby had earlier played out ⁠a warning that anyone taking part in the protest ⁠was committing a criminal offence.
A small group of Orange Order members wearing traditional silk orange sashes and black bowler hats gathered in another part of the town, a picture posted on X by Democratic Unionist Party ‌(DUP) lawmaker Carla Lockhart showed.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm, saying there have been “big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don’t want to see things go backwards”.
Jon Boutcher, the head of Northern Ireland police, called for “those with influence to encourage people to comply with the law”, referring to the protest blocking the Garvaghy Road. He said there have been no signs of violence or disorder.
“Police are engaging and working with all parties and will continue to do so. It is incumbent on us all to come together at times like this to do all we can to preserve a peaceful Northern Ireland.”
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, from the DUP, which supports Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, said on Sunday that threats of violence were unacceptable. “No one in Northern Ireland wants violence or disorder,” she added.
The Irish government said it was “very concerned” about the situation and that its priority was to avoid “a return to the divisions of the past”.
The Orange Order is a Protestant organisation closely associated with unionism, the political tradition that favours Northern Ireland remaining in the UK.
The Parades Commission, the independent body that rules on disputed marches in Northern Ireland, approved Sunday’s procession with a 35-person limit, barred bands and accompanying supporters, and required the march to finish by 9:30am (08:30 GMT).
The dispute over the Drumcree parade and Garvaghy Road became one of the most bitter marching confrontations of the “Troubles”, the decades-long conflict over Northern Ireland’s political status that largely ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
Repeated attempts by the Orange Order to return from Drumcree Parish Church along Garvaghy Road triggered protests, violence and major security operations during the 1990s.

articles.title_orig: A ‘Big Problem’: Trump’s War With Iran Drags Down Republicans in Midterms
articles.title_zh: A ‘Big Problem’: Trump’s War With Iran Drags Down Republicans in Midterms
articles.content_orig:
At least 17 members of Congress have called on the president to end the war.
Several Republicans running in competitive statewide and federal races are joining growing calls in their party to end the war in Iran with less than 40 days until the midterm elections.
As of Friday, 17 incumbent congressional Republicans running for re-election or non-incumbent candidates for Senate or governor's seats have called for an end to the war, either through votes in Congress to rein in President Donald Trump’s war powers or in statements on the campaign trail or online.
This comes as diesel fuel prices have jumped by nearly 60% since the conflict began at the end of February and as voters sour on the president -- a CNN poll conducted last week found 67% of Americans disapproved of Trump's job performance and 73% disapproved of how he was handling the situation in Iran. And 73% of Americans said that the war with Iran was having a negative effect on their financial situation, including 59% of Republicans.
Since the war in Iran started, Congress has voted on resolutions calling on Trump to get Congress' approval to continue hostilities in Iran. Of the 20 resolutions voted on, some Republicans have voted with Democrats five times to pass resolutions, though they don't force the president to do anything.
The GOP candidates who have broken with Trump on the war include six incumbent members of Congress running for reelection and five Republicans running in statewide races. Four of those five are currently in Congress and have voted against the war powers resolutions.
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, a former congressman, cut an ad on Monday saying, "The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly. When it does, energy costs will plummet." He has since said that any deal to end the war must ensure Iran can't build a nuclear weapon, Trump's stated goal for the conflict.
In Wisconsin, Rep. Tom Tiffany, the GOP nominee for governor, told ABC affiliate WISN on Wednesday, "it's time to move on."
"The president has final say in regards to this, but I just believe that we should be exiting Iran -- that it's time to move on," Tiffany said. "We've degraded their nuclear facilities. We degraded their military. Most of their ships are in the bottom of the ocean. Time to come home, take care of business here in America."
Tiffany's opponent, Democrat Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, put out an ad this week that slammed the congressman for voting in lockstep with the president on the war.
"Five times he has had the chance to end the war that’s driving our prices up, and five times he’s chosen Trump instead. Tom Tiffany’s only loyal to Trump -- not us, Wisconsin,” Crowley said in a press release.
Ohio Republican Sen. John Husted, facing a tight race for reelection, told Politico on Tuesday, "The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices," but he again voted against a war powers resolution on Thursday.
Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running in a tight Senate race, has voted against war powers resolutions, but reversed her position on Monday, calling for an "immediate end" to the war.
"Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran," she wrote. "We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices. … These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”
A day later, she insisted the House return to Washington, D.C. to address rising fuel prices, promising to "work with anyone to deliver."
“The House should return to DC immediately to work to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax, fully unleash E15 and biodiesel, and work on a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers," Hinson wrote on X .
House Speaker Mike Johnson last week canceled the two remaining weeks of its session and let the House leave early, saying, "It's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people to go and explain all the great things we've done."
Hinson's Democratic opponent Josh Turek, a state lawmaker, responded on X , "It's easy to send a tweet but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to. You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week."
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries criticized the Republicans who have recently broken with Trump on the war during a news conference Wednesday, saying that several of them are "on the verge of losing."
"Where were these Republican sycophants over the last six-plus months?" he said.
Iowa Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, who had opposed the war powers resolution but voted in favor of it last week, said in a statement, "Americans do not want another forever war."
She cited her military service and acknowledged the rising gas prices driven by the war in Iran, saying that Iowans are "paying too much at the pump."
And Iowa Republican Rep. Zach Nunn voted against previous war powers resolutions but broke with the president on the most recent vote.
"Iowa has already paid a devastating price, including two service members killed by an Iranian drone in Kuwait."
Nunn also recently demanded action on diesel prices, writing on X on Monday , "My plan: Sell American energy to Americans first. Pass my Iowa-led biofuel bill = bring down gas 50 cents. Hold Big Oil accountable for gouging," Nunn wrote.
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa, Jonathan Parker, Laura Peller and John Parkinson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.title_zh: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.content_orig:
An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.
Supporters had gathered outside her building overnight on Friday, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received.
Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners.
The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to fierce public anger.
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction, some setting off flares. They carried placards reading “Not one more eviction, not one less neighbor, we are all Maricarmen” and “right to housing at a fair price.”
At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza, some pitching tents. They remained in place early Sunday as dozens of activists staged a sit-in. A model of a vulture, decrying so-called “vulture funds,” hung above the camp.
Earlier in the week, tenants unions and other housing groups held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza.
An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union.
Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation.
“They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.”
Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease.
“We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction.
Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment.
The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing.
The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.”
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing.
Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she is worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city.
“Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.”
Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said she was currently looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs, but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available.
“Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.”
Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe.
“It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News.
It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with  politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.”
“Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”
Jamie Gray is a senior desk editor for NBC News based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_zh: At least 27 people killed in two shootings in South African townships
articles.content_orig:
Gunmen torched vehicles as they fled the scene of a mass shooting at bar near Johannesburg
Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.
Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.
In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks.
In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.
Police said thirteen men and four women were killed.
Deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to AFP news agency.
Speaking at the scene, he said police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects.
In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.
No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.
The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.

articles.title_zh: The Asian Games should be called the 'China Games' as its domination continues
articles.content_orig:
China's Song Jiayuan, right, and Zhang Linru hold their flags after competing in the women's shot put final at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Credit: AP/Lee Jin-man
NAGOYA, Japan — They're called the Asian Games. But more aptly, they should be called the “China Games,” another chapter in country’s four-decade domination of the continental, multisports championships.
Midway through the two-week event, China has won 107 gold medals with Japan on 31 in second place. The overall medal total is closer, but China still leads Japan 176 to 129 through Saturday's results.
These Asian Games involve at least 11,000 athletes. That's more than the Summer Olympics two years ago in Paris with about 10,700. And similar to the Olympics, the gap is very wide between the sporting haves, and the have-nots.
At the bottom of the medal table, four countries have only one bronze medal — Bangladesh, Brunei, Mongolia and Syria. And another half dozen countries have yet to win any medals
The six-day swimming competition dominated the first week, and here China piled up 30 golds. Freestyler Zhang Zhanshuo won seven golds and four came in every freestyle distance: the 200-meter, 400, 800 and 1,500. He also added gold in three relays.

Chinese 13-year-old Yu Zidi picked up three golds — 200 butterfly and the 200 and 400 individual medleys. Both swimmers will be forces at the world championships next year in Budapest, Hungary, and the Los Angeles Olympics the year after that.
Despite China's power, the only world record went to Japan's Shin Ohashi, who set the world mark in the 200 breaststroke (2 minutes, 4.83 seconds).
The flags of China and Japan are raised during the medal ceremony for the men's rings final in artistic gymnastics at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: AP/Eugene Hoshiko
It has been rough sailing for organizers and the Olympic Council of Asia. Organizers decided against building a dedicated athletes village, a move to contain spending. Instead, athletes and officials have been lodged on a cruise ship, in hotels, and in temporary wood huts.
Early complaints included beds that are too short, leaky roofs, and mix-ups in room assignment with women booked in with men.
Attendance has also been sparse in some venues, and transportation has been spotty with some venues located far from host city Nagoya.
Organizers have openly apologized.
Gold medalist, China team, pose with their national flag, after the women's 4 x 200-meter freestyle relay final in swimming at the Asian Games in Tokyo, Japan, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: AP/Hiro Komae
“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport,” Satoshi Murate, organizing committee general secretary, told a Saturday news conference. “I frankly apologize for the mistakes.”
Japan won the bid for these games in 2016. That was before the pandemic, before the Tokyo Olympics were delayed until 2021, and before bid scandals linked to the Tokyo Games were uncovered.
Momentum for big spending was lost.
The final price tag for the Tokyo Olympics was $ 13 billion, though a government audit suggested it was twice that much. In the wake, there was limited interests from sponsors and others to match that spending for the Asian Games.
Organizers were also embarrassed during the first week when the North Korean national anthem was played at a men's field hockey match between South Korea and Bangladesh.
Chances are you have never seen many of these sports. There's kabaddi, which looks like a physical game of tag, sepaktakraw (foot volleyball), kurash (wrestling with roots in Uzbekistan), jiu jitsu, padel, soft tennis, teqball and wushu.
Of course, there are all the old Olympic standbys such as track and field, tennis, swimming, badminton, gymnastics, soccer, cycling, weightlifting, and so forth.
Esports are also in the Asian Games for the second time following the games in China three years ago. On Saturday 11-year-old Japanese schoolboy Yuki Kurihara won a gold medal.
Mixed martial arts is also being included for the first time with a long-shot eye at landing in the Olympics.
The version in the Asian Games can be described as “MMA Light,” fighting without the cage. Fighters wear gloves and shin pads, elbow blows are banned, and no knees or kicks to the head are allowed when a fighter is on the ground.

articles.title_orig: Jalen Brunson makes Knicks history hosting ‘SNL’ season 52 premiere
articles.title_zh: Jalen Brunson makes Knicks history hosting ‘SNL’ season 52 premiere
articles.content_orig:
NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live.”
During Saturday’s hoops-heavy show, Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during Knicks’ NBA Finals games.
“The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.”
The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.
Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL'
“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”
Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.
“Can you foul out of ‘SNL?’” Towns asked.
In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson portrayed a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”
It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.
The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than the ones of Culhane’s character. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.
Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.
He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.
Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players , Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.
Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.
The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.
Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed season two of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

articles.title_orig: 2 giant pandas set off to Atlanta zoo from China after Xi-Trump summit
articles.title_zh: 2 giant pandas set off to Atlanta zoo from China after Xi-Trump summit
articles.content_orig:
Pandas departed Chengdu for their new homes in Georgia as part of agreement between Chinese and US governments
Two giant pandas departed Chengdu in south-western China early on Sunday for their new homes in Atlanta , Georgia, as part of an agreement between the Chinese and US governments.
While in Washington DC for a three - day summit with Donald Trump , Chinese president Xi Jinping announced that the pandas would arrive in Atlanta in the coming days. The loan of the pandas to the Atlanta zoo was one of the few concrete outcomes to come out of Xi’s state visit with the US president, which saw expressions of goodwill between the leaders, but no fixes to any of the longstanding differences between the two countries.
Atlanta said farewell to its last pandas in 2024, leaving the zoo without the bears. The new agreement was announced back in April, but without any dates.
Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the two adult pandas that will be on loan to Zoo Atlanta for 10 years as part of the agreement. Both pandas were born in 2020 and were kept at the Chengdu research base of giant panda breeding. Ping Ping, the male, has dark black circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang, the female, has a forehead that protrudes a bit, according to the Xinhua News Agency.
China has long used the pandas as part of its diplomacy globally, deploying the bears in loan programs as expressions of goodwill and letting loan agreements lapse when tensions arise.
Xi had said the loan program was an example of “friendship between the Chinese and Americans”.

articles.title_zh: New York Knicks’ Jalen Brunson kicks off the new season of ‘SNL’ tonight
articles.content_orig:
NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live.”
During Saturday’s hoops-heavy show, Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during the Knicks’ Finals games.
“The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.”
The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.
Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL'
“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”
Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.
“Can you foul out of ‘SNL’?” Towns asked.
In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson played a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”
It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with an over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.
The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than Culhane’s character’s. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.
Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.
He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.
Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players , Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.
Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.
The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.
Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed Season 2 of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia’s army promises restraint amid fears of new civil war
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia’s army promises restraint amid fears of new civil war
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia faces renewed war as armed groups launch offensive
Ethiopia’s federal military has said it is handling rising tensions in the country’s north with restraint, as fears grow that Ethiopia could be heading towards another civil war.
In his first comments on the recent military developments, Army Chief of Staff Field Marshal Berhanu Jula said the army was responding to what he called provocations from the Tigray front with “wisdom and restraint”.
He accused Eritrea of funding and supporting armed groups to weaken Ethiopia, describing the “Tsimdo” alliance as an extension of a longstanding pattern of hostile alliances, which he said cannot confront the state without outside backing.
Eritrea, wary that landlocked Ethiopia may be seeking to invade it to gain access to the Red Sea, denied the accusations.
The fighting has spread from Tigray into neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions after seven armed groups announced an alliance , the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, committed to removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
In Afar, the latest battles have taken place around Abala, where the military has been trying to prevent rebels from seizing control.
Separately, in North Wollo, a zone of Amhara bordering Tigray, the army said on Thursday it had killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 in a counter-offensive, reporting heavy losses for the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
The TPLF’s Tigray Army said the federal government had launched a “full-scale offensive” involving infantry, mechanised units and drones.
Abdisalam Balema, a TPLF central committee member, told Al Jazeera the situation had become a “full war”.
Fighting has also continued around Sama, Soqota and Raya Alamata, with government forces reportedly closing in on the town of Alamata.
The army command said it prefers a strategy of “strategic calm” over a large-scale military confrontation , arguing the Tigray front’s popular support is dwindling and its leadership divided.
Internet access was reportedly cut across northern Ethiopia on Friday, a day after the UN said it was alarmed by reports of drones being used against civilians there.
The renewed fighting has put the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray, under severe strain. It comes weeks after Washington lifted sanctions on Ethiopia and Eritrea tied to atrocities from the last war, saying the “national emergency … has expired”.
It marks the most serious challenge yet to that agreement, raising fears of a wider regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across Ethiopia.
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Ethiopia’s president sought to portray the country as a force for regional stability, accusing unnamed external actors of meddling in Ethiopia’s affairs while highlighting Addis Ababa’s role in supporting peace efforts in neighbouring Sudan.
Alemayehu Weldemariam, a professor of law at Indiana University, told Al Jazeera that the federal government bears much of the blame for the collapse of the Pretoria Agreement.
“This war has been in the making for a while now. Much of the provisions in the cessation of hostilities [in the 2022 agreement] were primarily sabotaged by the federal government itself,” he said, citing fuel, service and cash restrictions imposed on Tigray, and the government’s failure to set up the interim administration the deal had promised.
“What was supposed to be an interim arrangement turned out to be permanent,” with Tigray excluded from national elections since, he added.

After a wild first few weeks of the college football season, we had our best slate yet in Week 4 and it did not disappoint.
The day started with a marquee showdown between No. 1 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee , and the Longhorns won rights to the 'UT' moniker with a tough defensive performance. Texas' Colin Simmons tied a school record with five sacks in a 20-17 win — though he did get in a bit of trouble after his first .
No. 17 Iowa provided the drama for the day in the afternoon, driving the length of the field in the final minute and scoring on a walk-off TD pass from Hank Brown to Reece Vander Zee as time expired to beat No. 18 Michigan 20-19 . Elsewhere, No. 4 Ole Miss got shelled by No. 21 Florida , No. 2 Georgia throttled Oklahoma in an ugly game for Sooners QB John Mateer and No. 15 Utah held on for a 31-17 win at Iowa State .
In the evening, No. 20 Oregon kept its conference title and playoff hopes alive with a clutch road win at No. 12 USC, but paid a price. QB Dante Moore was knocked out of the game after a scary collision . Dylan Raiola replaced him and led the Ducks to an impressive 41-27 win .
In other action, Lane Kiffin and No. 10 LSU bounced back after their disappointing loss to Ole Miss last week with a beatdown of No. 23 Texas A&M and No. 8 Alabama rolled to a 49-18 win over South Carolina .
Follow all of the action with live updates, highlights and analysis below:

articles.title_orig: Takeaways from College Football Week 4: Raiola rises to the occasion; Jeremiah Smith's Heisman moment?
articles.title_zh: Takeaways from College Football Week 4: Raiola rises to the occasion; Jeremiah Smith's Heisman moment?
articles.content_orig:
College football is unpredictable and delightful, which is why we live for what happens on Saturdays. And Week 4 absolutely delivered, from a stunning last-second win for Iowa at the Big House to a big bounce-back performance from Oregon. Each Sunday, I’ll publish my biggest takeaways from the college football weekend. I’ll highlight the most interesting storylines, track College Football Playoff contenders and specifically shout out individual and team performances that deserve the spotlight.
When Raiola took his first snap of the game, you could still see the ambulance taking Oregon starting quarterback Dante Moore off the field in the top left corner of the screen. It was a jarring moment, much like the hit itself that knocked Moore out of the game and sent him to the hospital. It was an emotional and charged moment for both Oregon and USC, and it was an inflection point in the game. And Raiola, the former Nebraska quarterback, stepped in and put Oregon into the end zone two plays later. Raiola was impressive in relief overall, throwing for 289 yards and two touchdowns and leading the Ducks to a 41-27 win over the Trojans. Raiola deserves a lot of credit for deciding to go to Oregon, knowing he was unlikely to start if Moore came back to college. He was willing to sit and learn, and by doing that, he helped the Ducks face — and survive — a challenge that would have been far more daunting without a QB2 with 22 career starts to his name.
Lather, rinse and repeat: USC’s defense let it down in a big moment against an elite team in a gotta-have-it game. It was supposed to be better. It was supposed to be different. Gary Patterson was supposed to fix the defense. The talent was supposed to be better — the game plan, too. The time was supposed to be now for USC to finally win a big one, and the Trojans fell short against a backup quarterback. Dan Lanning continues to own the West Coast, and Lincoln Riley’s seat continues to heat up.
Florida might be the most dangerous team in America. Don’t be late to the bandwagon.
The Longhorns played a nearly perfect fourth quarter against Ohio State, scoring 21 unanswered points to come all the way back and beat the Buckeyes. Outside of that, the Arch Manning-led offense has looked quite inconsistent. It’ll look good for a drive or two and then go totally ice-cold, which doesn’t make any sense considering the offensive weapons that Texas has on its roster. Or there might be some truly inexcusable penalties, like we saw on Saturday against Tennessee. How else do you explain a three-point win after you dominated so much of the game — and tallied 10 sacks? Oof.
Ohio State dialed up four touchdowns for No. 4 on Saturday, a fitting spotlight for the best offensive player in college football. As a rule, it’s hard for non-quarterbacks to win the Heisman Trophy. Their stats must be otherworldly, and they have to be the player given the credit for their team’s offensive success — not their quarterback. That last part could be an issue for the Buckeyes, who also have a Heisman contender in Julian Sayin. I don’t think that will hurt Smith’s chances to get to New York City as a finalist, but it could hurt him when it comes to actually winning the award. Either way, he deserves the trip. And those four touchdowns from Saturday help boost the stat line for voters who care about that. The rest of ‘em should just watch him week-to-week. You’ll see all you need to know.
I picked the Broncos to make the CFP in my preseason bracket, and they have done nothing but make me look good ever since. A close loss at Oregon, a lopsided win over Memphis (out of the American) and a dominant victory over Western Michigan (last year’s MAC champion). They’ll be the heavy favorite to win the new-look Pac-12, and if they do that, they should be the highest-ranked G6 champion and the winner of the CFP auto-bid. And it’ll be well-deserved.
We all saw that coming, didn’t we?
One second, two seconds? Doesn’t matter. The football gods balanced out the karma from Week 1’s Hail (Bail?) Mary with Iowa’s come-from-behind win over Michigan on Saturday. And that sets up a massive game in Iowa City next weekend with the Buckeyes coming to town.

articles.title_orig: College football winners, losers in Week 4: Iowa emerges as Big Ten title threat, John Mateer struggles again
articles.title_zh: College football winners, losers in Week 4: Iowa emerges as Big Ten title threat, John Mateer struggles again
articles.content_orig:
Week 4 marks the formal start of conference play across college football , and the big-time matchups delivered. No. 17 Iowa pulled a stunner against No. 18 Michigan to win at Michigan Stadium for the first time since 2010 on the last play.
But while there's been plenty of highs, a few high-profile players struggled in big moments. Trinidad Chambliss was unable to keep up the magic against Florida , while Oklahoma's John Mateer collapsed against Georgia . The ACC race also took a wild turn after Wake Forest upset Louisville .
In the night slate, a few more titans fell as No. 12 USC, No. 13 Penn State and No. 23 Texas A&M all dropped. The losses shake up conference title and postseason pictures, but can teams recover? Here are the biggest winners and losers of Week 4.
Expectations were low for the Aggies when they traveled to face No. 10 LSU. But in one fell swoop, a 35-6 loss, No. 23 Texas A&M's season effectively ended. Quarterback Marcel Reed was regrettably the primary culprit, completing a paltry 10 of 26 passes for 106 yards and an interception. The backup, Brady Hart, threw an interception on his only pass attempt.
As if that wasn't bad enough, Texas A&M allowed more than 300 yards passing and nearly 200 yards rushing. Frankly, the Aggies are just a bad football team at this point. Outside of a few talented wide receivers, who can't get the ball due to bad quarterback play, it's hard to find a single advantage Texas A&M can create against opponents.
No. 1 Texas, No. 8 Alabama and No. 14 Tennessee are still on the schedule, along with a road trip to Oklahoma. Will the Aggies make a bowl game?
The Cowboys officially turned the page on their season-opening loss to Tulsa by storming back from an early deficit to beat West Virginia 41-24 on the road. The Mountaineers were right on the edge of the rankings last week after beating No. 25 Virginia, and took a 14-3 lead early in the second quarter.
But when faced with adversity, quarterback Drew Mestemaker and wide receiver Wyatt Young again rose to the occasion. Young was unstoppable with eight catches for 192 yards and a touchdown in the win. Mestemaker shook off an interception to finish with 389 yards on only 27 pass attempts, 270 yards of which came in the second half.
The win over West Virginia was Oklahoma State's first Big 12 win in more than 1,000 days, snapping an 18-game losing streak. The last win was amazingly before the Cowboys played in the 2023 Big 12 title game. A new era is afoot.
Once again, USC was presented with the opportunity to get over the hump. After knocking Dante Moore out of the game with a dirty play, they were even playing at home against a backup quarterback. But when the game was decided, the Trojans were again too soft.
USC faced multiple opportunities to extend drives, but went 2 of 11 on third down. The Trojans failed to contain backup Dylan Raiola on fourth down and got bullied in high-leverage spots. This Trojans team is young, but excuses just keep piling up every year. With No. 5 Indiana, No. 7 Ohio State and No. 13 Penn State left on the schedule, when will it happen?
The Badgers needed something positive to happen in the Luke Fickell era. Old Dominion quarterback transfer Colton Joseph was ready to deliver. In the last 3:31, Joseph threw two touchdown passes to stun No. 13 Penn State, including a 72-yard pass to Jacob Harris with only 73 seconds remaining. It was the most complete defensive performance we've seen the Badgers put together, holding Penn State to only 233 yards. This was the kind of game Fickell was hired to win. There's a long season ahead, but can Fickell build on it?
Iowa's win against No. 18 Michigan to stay undefeated was a perfect Kirk Ferentz football game. The Hawkeyes puttered about for the first 40 minutes of play, only staying within striking distance because of a 99-yard kickoff return for a touchdown. And then, Hank Brown came to life.
The Hawkeyes got one of the great plays in program history, a game-winning touchdown with no time left on the clock by Brown to Reece Vander Zee for an unbelievable touchdown. The win was the first for Iowa in Michigan Stadium since 2010. More importantly, it seriously launched the No. 17 Hawkeyes into the Big Ten title and postseason conversation. With conference frontrunners Ohio State and Oregon already possessing losses, Iowa could easily crash the party.
Playing Georgia is never a recipe for success, but Oklahoma's QB1 put together one of the most stunningly poor performances of the season. After going down 14-0 in the second quarter, Mateer dropped one of the worst fumbles you'll ever see that turned third-and-goal into a Georgia defensive touchdown. He threw another interception, and then dropped the ball yet again to set up a short 11-yard touchdown drive for Georgia.
By the time the dust settled, Oklahoma was trailing 28-0 at halftime, part of a 41-13 loss against the Bulldogs in Athens. Statistically, Mateer was able to fight back in garbage time to finish with a respectable stat line, but the damage was done.
Oklahoma coach Brent Venables acknowledged that he considered making a change at halftime , but backup Whitt Newbauer has never played real snaps. There's no real answer on this Sooners roster, and Mateer is the face of the dysfunction.
CHRIS COLE HOUSE CALL 🏠 📺: ESPN pic.twitter.com/wNOacZCjqI
The Gators announced their return to major college football under Jon Sumrall on Saturday, finishing off an emphatic 52-28 win over No. 4 Ole Miss . The Gators obliterated the Rebels behind a combined 268 yards and four touchdowns rushing from Jadan Baugh and Duke Clark , finishing with more than 300 yards on the ground as a team.
While an emotional letdown was expected for the Rebels after the dramatic win over Lane Kiffin and LSU last weekend, Florida looks the part of a serious national contender for the first time in years. The Gators still have No. 1 Texas and No. 2 Georgia on the schedule, but the Florida team we saw in Week 4 can hang with anyone.
The Cardinals can't make anything easy. One week after taking control of the ACC championship race with a win over SMU, Louisville lost a stunner against a streaking Wake Forest squad 30-27. With the loss, the Cardinals are no longer an at-large contender for the College Football Playoff field with two early losses. SMU still has a shot, and there are a few loose undefeated ACC teams left, but Louisville looked like the top competition to Miami . Now, things are much more complicated.
Boise State officially took their place as kings of the Group of Six race after obliterating Western Michigan 32-7 in a marquee matchup. The Broncos were fantastic in the win, holding WMU to 3.8 yards per pass attempt and 2 of 11 on third down, while getting an efficient 204 yards and three touchdowns from Maddux Madsen . With wins over Memphis and Western Michigan, Boise State becomes the heavy favorite to reach the College Football Playoff -- if it can survive a stacked Pac-12.
Texas Tech put a lot of faith in Hammond coming off of an ACL tear, but the redshirt sophomore has struggled to meet the moment after taking over as the starter. Hammond threw three interceptions in the first half against Sam Houston and looked out of sorts as the Bearkats pulled within 21-14 at the half.
Hammond managed to get back on track in the second half, but it's been multiple games of inconsistent play for a team that hoped to contend for the Big 12 title. The running game got going in the second half, but teams just don't trust Hammond's downfield passing, and it's making life harder. The talent is there, but the consistency has to come soon with the heart of Big 12 play on the horizon.

Brunson's monologue had a mix of lessons he learned on his way to winning a championship and interaction with his teammates.
Stiller took to X and expressed how impressive Brunson was hosting.
"BEST MONOLOGUE EVER," Stiller tweeted.
The actor also posted other tweets on Brunson's SNL hosting.
The NBA player also took part in a few sketches, showcasing how diverse his acting skills are.

China's research icebreaker Xuelong is part of its growing expansion in Antarctica. ( Huang Taoming/Xinhua via AFP )
China is preparing to build its sixth research station in Antarctica, expanding into Marie Byrd Land — a remote, little-studied stretch of the continent's west.
It has some experts and politicians worried.
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie is among those concerned about Australia's defence priorities.
"Five bases have already been built, and China claims there is no geopolitical motive," she said.
Whether that alarm is warranted depends on who you ask.
A new radio telescope installed by China's Antarctica team. ( Xinhua via AFP )
China says the new base, which it plans to build next year, will support research into climate change, ice sheets and marine systems.
And it is far from the only country with a significant presence.
The US operates three permanent year-round bases. So does Australia, which claims 42 per cent of the continent, while Russia has five year-round stations.
But experts warn what matters most is not the station itself.
It is what the project might signal about China's deepening influence inside the institutions that govern Antarctica.
China's proposed new station is in Marie Byrd Land. ( ABC News: Cordelia Brown )
Jiliang Chen, a lecturer in Antarctic law and governance at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania, sees the new station mainly as a matter of prestige.
"Building a station is China capitalising on its strength in this strategic game," Mr Chen said.
China's new station is being developed as per the Antarctic Treaty System's environmental assessment procedures.
Under the Antarctic Treaty, member states cannot veto a proposed new station.
The treaty was originally signed by 12 countries in 1959 and designed to ensure the use of the area for peaceful purposes only and the protection of the environment.
China's scientific expedition team constructing Qinling Station two years ago. ( Zhou Yuan/Xinhua via AFP )
Mr Chen said a stronger physical presence helped consolidate China's role in future decisions on the continent.
"It gives people one more thing to be proud of, scientists more facilities to do research, and more projects to plan," he said.
One complication is that equipment such as satellite systems, communications hardware, aircraft and drones serve civilian research and can easily be adapted for military use.
That dual-use capability is why Mr Chen believes inspection and transparency matter most.
Other experts are more suspicious.
Elizabeth Buchanan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), points to China's existing satellite ground stations and its Military-Civil Fusion policy, which enables civilian companies to develop or supply technologies for military use.
Her deeper worry is that China's spread of stations could eventually let it operate across Antarctica without depending on other countries.
West Antarctica has not been heavily researched. ( Supplied: Matt Burke )
Some say that framing is overblown.
The Antarctic Treaty prohibits military bases, weapons and new territorial claims, while permitting military personnel and equipment for peaceful purposes.
China's embassy in Canberra told the ABC it was "fully committed to ensuring its activities in the region strictly align with the Antarctic Treaty System".
Tony Press, the former head of the Australian Antarctic Division, said he believed mining and military fears were exaggerated, citing the cost and difficulty of moving people and equipment across such a hostile environment.
Unlike China's year-round Quinling station , the new base would run only in summer, hardly the profile of a strategic outpost, Mr Press said.
Instead, he said China was making a geopolitical statement.
"China is obviously doing the old strategic thing of making sure they've got stations around Antarctica that demonstrate quite clearly that they are a big player in, and have an interest in, all parts of Antarctica," he said.
China opened its fifth station, Qinling, in 2024. ( YouTube: China News Service )
Analysts say China is finding ways to become increasingly influential without breaking the rules.
China joined the treaty later than other countries, in 1983.
"China has always been nervous about natural resources and probably more hungry for economic growth," Mr Chen said.
Fishing is where this showed most clearly, he said.
China joined the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), largely because of its interest in Antarctic fishing, Mr Chen said.
China has invested in icebreakers alongside building new bases. ( Huang Taoming/Xinhua via AFP )
Ms Buchanan pointed to the broader growth of China's fishing fleet and domestically built fleet of icebreakers as part of its "Polar Silk Road" strategy.
She said China was also preparing to unveil a nuclear-powered icebreaker, which she said would reduce its reliance on gateway ports such as Hobart.
China is limiting the size of its high sea fishing fleet, except for the polar regions, Mr Chen said.
Antarctic krill fishing is an exception in China's plan for high sea fishing.
Many of Antarctica's emperor penguin colonies have suffered increased or total breeding failure. ( Supplied: Klein & Hubert/WWF )
China has generally opposed new marine protected areas in Antarctica.
Nearly half of Antarctica's 60 emperor penguin colonies have suffered increased or total breeding failure since 2016 as sea ice they depend on has retreated, according to researchers from the British Antarctic Survey.
Efforts to list them as a Special Protected Species have stalled at CCAMLR, blocked by China and Russia.
The stated objections cite insufficient scientific evidence, or argue that such a listing would address a symptom (habitat loss) rather than its underlying cause of climate change, which sits outside the treaty's scope.
Lyn Goldsworthy, an adjunct researcher at the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies, said China was operating from a strategic perspective, and wanted to avoid restricting access to certain areas in case it had "certain aspirations" in the future.
Ms Goldsworthy added China appeared to join the conservation body CCAMLR for the purpose of fishing first, not marine biology or conservation.
Krill is another source of tension.
The tiny crustaceans are a primary food source for penguins and whales.
Next month's CCAMLR meeting, known as the "Krill Convention", will debate fishing limits.
China has a particular interest in Antarctic krill, which is increasingly valuable as an ingredient in aquaculture feed and nutritional supplements.
Emperor penguins have suffered after record-low Antarctic sea ice. ( Supplied: Bryan and Cherry Alexander/WWF )
Krill products were pulled from shelves in Australian supermarkets after environmental campaigns, but China and Norway are pushing to raise the current catch limit much higher.
Ms Goldsworthy described years of stalemate.
"You have China saying, 'We don't believe in marine protected areas, you should give us our krill fishery'. Other countries are saying, 'No, we won't discuss krill fishery expansion until we've progressed marine protected areas,'" she said.
"There is now a deep distrust."
The underlying ecological concern that over-concentration of fishing in certain areas damages predator populations and habitats has become inseparable from the geopolitics around it, Ms Goldsworthy said.
One flashpoint was an area where heavy Chinese fishing activity overlapped with an Argentine-Chilean proposal for a marine protected area, she said.
Experts say Russia has also played a "disruptive" role, objecting alongside China to new marine protection sites.
China has been increasing its number of bases for scientific research. ( Xinhua via AFP )
